about: What we have learned about prompting for each goal. The studio adds `wording` to a description, shows `tips`, and warns about `trouble` words. The CLI and MCP server read this same file.

character.label: A moving character
character.wording: full body, front view, standing in an A-pose, arms straight and angled down about 45 degrees with a clear gap from the body, hands open, palms facing down, empty hands, feet slightly apart, eyes open, slightly larger, clearly defined eyes with visible eyelids, plain light grey background, soft even studio lighting
tips: One character, whole body, standing in an A-pose: arms angled down about 45°, with a gap between arms and body. The pose words are added for you.
Empty hands. Make swords and shields as separate props.
A soft 3D-render look gives cleaner faces than flat anime or cel art.
Say what you want, not what you don't: "smooth fabric", not "no wrinkles". Naming a thing tends to add it.
Skip capes, long coats, robes and aprons if you will rig it. Loose cloth tears when it moves.
Describe the look and materials ("rusty iron armour", "leather boots"), not a scene.
Plain light background, soft even light, no dramatic shadows.
More in the picture guide.

creature.label: A moving creature
creature.wording: one creature alone, full body, three-quarter front view, standing still on all of its legs in a calm neutral pose, symmetrical body, legs straight and planted flat on the ground with clear gaps between them, head straight and looking forward, stylised 3D game creature, plain light grey background, soft even studio lighting
tips: One creature, whole body, standing still on all its legs. The pose words are added for you: the move comes later, from a video.
Say what it has: "four legs, two bat wings and a long tail". Its body is copied as drawn, so the 3D model and its rig follow these words.
Wings: say how it holds them, the same way on both sides, such as "wings folded at its sides" or "wings half open and level".
A creature drawn flying, rearing or turning its head comes out lopsided in 3D. The studio measures it and offers another picture.
Plain light background, soft even light, no dust, fire or glow.

prop.label: A prop
prop.wording: single object, whole object in view, centred, plain light grey background, soft even studio lighting
tips: One object, all of it in view, in the middle of the picture.
Say what it is made of: oak, iron, glass, stone.
Plain light background. No smoke, glow trails or motion blur: the 3D step needs one clean shape.

set.label: A prop set
set.wording: a 3x3 grid of nine separate objects, same art style, clear gaps between them, each object whole and centred in its cell, plain light grey background
tips: Ask for a 3×3 grid of nine separate objects in one style.
Leave clear gaps between them so they can be cut apart.
Name the nine things in reading order (top row first) so each prop gets the right name.

picture.label: A picture
tips: Anything goes for a picture you only want to look at.
If you might turn it into 3D later, follow the Character or Prop tips now.

upload.label: Your own picture
tips: A plain or cut-out background works best.
The whole subject in view, front or three-quarter angle.
At least 768 px, with no text or logos over it.
For characters you want to animate: a T-pose with empty hands.

trouble.message: Loose cloth can tear or stretch when the character moves. Leave it out for the cleanest rig.
Held items get rigged as part of the hand. Make them as separate props instead.
A pose other than an A-pose makes rigging harder. The A-pose wording is added for you.
Long hair, tails and wings may not rig well yet.
A creature drawn in motion comes out lopsided in 3D and rigs badly. It is drawn standing still (added for you); the move comes later, from a video.
Effects like glow, smoke or fire don't turn into clean 3D. Describe the object, not the effect.
A scene behind the subject confuses the 3D step. Ask for a plain background (added for you).
